children.author: vickychijwani
children.text:
I feel the same way. Apart from accessibility and generalization, there is another important difference in marginal costs - unlike physical goods, mass production of software doesn’t require the programmer to churn away at the tools (LLMs) to produce more copies of them.

Mass production of physical goods carried a marginal cost in inputs AND time for those workers. Software carries negligible marginal costs (e.g., direct serving costs) - except of course a small subset of software that uses LLMs at runtime, which again carries non-trivial marginal power costs, at least as of 2026.

The fundamental difference is that Looms were point process automation that cost capital. They took a job a person did and made it automatic so that the person could be fired in exchange for up front cost.

The weaver couldn't build the machine, maintain it, adapt it, take it home, use it for other processes, try their own creative designs, open a competing shop, work in other textiles etc.

But agentic tools are not that. They DO allow all that. In fact software engineering has always been about automating things, and agentic tools just allow more people to automate more things, AND create more software the way they want it.

LLMs just don't feel like a loom. They feel something that can be used by workers themselves. Like power tools. A very generic power tool. That's essentially free. Unlike all automation to date which required massive up front capital to automate one single process.

Maybe that's the difference - accessibility and generalization.

What fundamental difference are you pointing at between looms and computers here? Both let you do craft faster.

Note that it took some time before workers' wages actually collapsed.

children.author: tsss
children.text: If those people have their way then their children or grandchildren will just be conquered by another nation with better tech and killed. That ideology can't survive in the long term.

I have said it before, Luddism is a civilization ending disease. If this type of people have their way we will have very little to no new tech because most tech is automation and doing things faster and with less energy than before. We most probably need some kind of AI guidance for deep space travel, Luddites would prevent humans from reaching the other planets and stars, cures to diseases found by AI, etc etc.

I think the Luddites' beef was more about losing options, as they watched their sense of agency in their lives and careers slip away. They couldn't rent their own automated looms for the equivalent of $20/month. Those things were expensive, exotic machines usable only in industrial settings, more like NVL72 racks than RTX 5090s. But with AI, we are as you suggest gaining options, so any comparison with Luddism fails from the get-go.

Obviously the correct way to view the arrival of AI is as an empowering tool for the ultimate benefit of us all, but just as obviously there are a lot of people who simply don't seem capable of understanding that. Obviously the correct way to react to the arrival of AI is to severely regulate the monopolists and oligarchs rather than the technology itself, but... see above.

Unfortunately there is no obvious way to deal with people who think the Luddites were somehow morally superior, or who otherwise want to rehabilitate or emulate them. It's like flashing back to late 2019, watching news reports come in about some sort of weird, unusually-severe flu that seemed to be spreading. Nobody knew for sure what to do then, and I don't think anyone does now. But we are going to have to do something to keep those people from dragging us backward with the self-centered psychological pandemic they are trying to spread.

children.text:
Of course someone will be in the line of responsibility (blame) for software reliability. That person will also use automation to make their job / life easier. And they'll insist on changes to the stack to make it more reliable and performant. And there will still be proven offerings by large companies for profitable niches.

But the Luddite question is not existence but scale. Can all 4 million software engineers find jobs if this is all that's left of software engineering. Also dunno

In my opinion LLMs can write code but they don't replace human skill and judgement in software engineering.

They can help you make decisions but ultimately humans still have to be responsible.

When your payments gateway goes down the week before Christmas you can't just say "well Claude did that, I have no idea how it works or why it can't handle the traffic".

The LLM bros want to claim that role will be handled by... who? The CEO is going to start prompting Claude at 3am making random changes in production to fix the payments gateway? The product manager? The cleaner?

Or you have some agent loop constantly making random changes in production to crucial core parts of your codebase with no human supervision?

I just can't see how actual software engineers who understand how the system works aren't still needed

source.text:
I got coffee with a nice person from HN today. They were wearing a hat with the word "Luddite" on it. I knew what it meant but asked anyway - yes it's not anti-tech, it's anti automation and loss of craft.

The thing about luddites is that yes they wanted to preserve human craftsmanship, and as you say it didn't work. John Henry died. Luddites worked in factories and declined into poverty. Hopeless. Doomed.

But, I am cranking down my personal backlog with AI tools, using them at work, and loving the usefulness of them. It doesn't feel like I'm a master weaver who has their work automated, it feels like I'm reaping productivity gains.

Was there ever a moment in the Luddite movement when some of them leaned in and had fun? Did some of John Henry's colleagues just really enjoy the new steam drivers?

It doesn't _feel_ like I'm being forced out of my trade. I sincerely doubt the Luddites had a moment where they happily shelled out the 1820 equivalent of $20/m to get access to a weaving machine. I'm not saying "this time is different", but I am saying everyone tells me to not use AI, and to be afraid, and I'm de-skilling or whatever, etc. How do we all _know_ what is right?

A loom does not bring agency. It takes it. But I feel like having a computer, access to LLM, increases my agency just a bit. It allows me to do more, not just do what I need to _faster_. It's not _just_ automation.
